strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes a genuine and practically important failure mode — Marginal Path Collapse — in ratio-of-densities steering of diffusion/flow models, which prior Feynman–Kac corrector work implicitly assumed away.

The Path Existence Criterion (Theorem 2.1/B.1) is clean, tractable (only requires checking positivity of scalar coefficients C_k(t) computable from analytic schedules), and demonstrably sharp: the boundary case C(t)=0 is shown to admit both collapse and existence via a concrete 1D example (Example B.1), elevating the result beyond a generic sufficient condition.

The ACE method is constructively grounded: Theorem B.2 gives an explicit bump-function construction guaranteeing path existence, and Theorem A.1 derives the correct weighted SDE/ODE with time-varying exponents via Ito calculus, including auxiliary log-density dynamics; FKC is recovered as the constant-exponent special case, making the contribution a principled generalization rather than an ad hoc heuristic.

Experimental evidence is broad and well-controlled: a synthetic checker benchmark with distributional metrics across 5 seeds, flexible-pose scaffold decoration and fragment linking on CrossDocked2020 beating both steering baselines (NR, FKC) and specialized monolithic models (Delete, AutoFragDiff, FFLOM), ablations against heuristic time-varying schedules and time-reparameterization, a 125-composition prevalence study (41%–80% collapse rates), and a homogeneous-regime image composition experiment showing gains even without collapse.

Good scientific hygiene: appendix proves the claimed criterion via Gaussian-envelope bounds (Proposition B.2, Lemma B.3), includes honest limitations (Gaussian-prior/compact-support assumption, linear scaling with expert count, steering-not-model-repair scope), ablations that disentangle time-variation per se from validity-preserving design, a reproducibility statement with code, and an appropriate impact statement discussing dual-use risks.
weaknesses: The central theory relies on Gaussian-prior-to-compactly-supported-target assumptions, but real pretrained experts (EDM, GeoDiff, DiffSBDD) do not exactly satisfy compact support, and the practical guarantee inherits score/velocity approximation errors; the gap between the idealized criterion and the empirical molecular systems is acknowledged but not quantified.

The bump-function hyperparameters (B1, B2) are effectively hand-tuned per guidance scale (footnote 5: distinct B2 for each omega in the scaffold task; large B1 values in Table 2), and Table 2 exhibits high variance for several ACE configurations, raising questions about robustness and how a practitioner would select these without trial and error.

Fragment linking is evaluated with a single random seed, and the comparison with fixed-pose specialized baselines (Delete, AutoFragDiff) is not fully apples-to-apples since ACE uses a more permissive flexible-pose formulation; the OSR advantage partly reflects the relaxed problem, though the NR/FKC comparisons are well controlled.

Guarantees are of path existence, not sample quality; the concentration result (Proposition 2.1/E.1) is an informal quantile-radius bound that motivates but does not fully explain when larger C(t) helps versus amplifies network approximation error — the trade-off is discussed only empirically.

Presentation has minor flaws: an informal main-text proposition, typos in Figure 1 ('Adaptive path Correction'), and the reliance on Appendix E for several substantive claims (prevalence study, reparameterization comparison) that would strengthen the main narrative.

strengths: Identifies and formalizes a genuine failure mode (Marginal Path Collapse) for heterogeneous ratio-of-densities steering, which prior Feynman–Kac corrector work (Skreta et al., 2025a) implicitly assumes away; this is a clear and useful conceptual contribution.

The Path Existence Criterion (Theorem B.1) is clean and, under its stated assumptions (Gaussian-prior stochastic interpolants with compactly supported targets), is proved sharply: C_k(t) > 0 suffices for integrability and C_k(t) < 0 at any coordinate implies collapse, with the boundary case C(t)=0 handled via a concrete counterexample (Example B.1).

The ACE sampling dynamics (Theorem A.1/2.3) are derived carefully via Fokker–Planck/Ito arguments, correctly add the γ̇_i(t) log q̃ terms needed for time-varying exponents, and provably reduce to FKC when exponents are constant; Algorithm 1 vs Algorithm 2 makes the delta transparent.

Experimental coverage is broad: a synthetic checkerboard benchmark with quantitative W1/W2/MMD metrics, flexible-pose scaffold decoration and fragment linking on CrossDocked2020 against both steering baselines (NR, FKC) and task-specific models (AutoFragDiff, Delete, FFLOM), a time-reparameterization baseline (Appendix E.6), heuristic time-varying schedule baselines (Appendix C.3), a schedule-collapse frequency study (125 compositions, Table E.10), and a homogeneous image-generation setting (COCO-MIG).

Ablations on ESS threshold and bump parameters (Tables C.2–C.5), a survey establishing that schedule heterogeneity is the norm in molecular diffusion models (Tables E.7–E.9), and an honest limitations/scope discussion (Appendix F and main text).
weaknesses: Theory–practice gap: The sharp PEC assumes exactly Gaussian-prior interpolants to compactly supported targets, but the deployed experts (EDM, GeoDiff, DiffSBDD) are learned models whose marginals satisfy these assumptions only approximately. The paper does not quantify how much model approximation error or non-compactness could violate the criterion's sharpness in the real molecular experiments, so the 'guaranteed path validity' claim is weaker in practice than stated.

The practical correction is a fairly crude heuristic: a two-parameter bump function (B1, B2) added to one exponent. Theorem B.2 only guarantees existence given C(0) > 0, and the same bump parameters also amplify score/velocity network errors (acknowledged in the sensitivity analysis), so the method introduces a nontrivial hyperparameter search burden whose principled resolution is not provided.

The truncation at t_end plus single Euler–Maruyama 'jump' to t=1 (Appendix B.3) discards the final interval of the composed path; the O((1−t_end)^2) error bound is asserted for a constant-drift approximation but no empirical measurement of this endpoint error is reported.

Some experiments are under-powered for the strength of the claims: fragment linking uses a single seed, schedule-comparison scaffolding uses 3 seeds, and the guidance-scale range (ω ∈ [1.1, 1.4]) is narrow; conclusions about 'scaling with guidance weight' rest on very small ω values.

Presentation defects: several figures have incomplete/broken labels (e.g., Fig. 3 axis annotations, Fig. 4 panel labels), the notation slips between γ̇_i(t) and γ_i in the method section, Table 2 mixes 'min' and 'mean±std' reporting non-standardly, and the reproduction statement's code URL appears to be missing/empty, undermining the reproducibility claim.

Originality is moderate: the core sampler is a direct generalization of existing Feynman–Kac correctors with an extra importance-weight term, and time-varying guidance schedules exist in prior CFG work; the novelty rests mainly on the collapse diagnosis and the existence criterion, which is specialized to the Gaussian/compact-support regime.

The homogeneous-regime image gains (Appendix E.7, +9.6%p on COCO-MIG) are attributed to Proposition 2.1's quantile-radius control, but this is an informal link; alternative explanations (e.g., stronger conditioning at intermediate times) are not disentangled beyond the B=5 choice.

strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes a genuine, previously undocumented failure mode (Marginal Path Collapse) in ratio-of-densities steering, with a clean motivating Gaussian example (Eq. 3, Fig. 2) showing that valid endpoints do not imply valid intermediate densities.

The Path Existence Criterion (Theorem 2.1 / B.1) is rigorously proven, with both sufficiency and necessity directions, a careful treatment of the boundary case C(t)=0 (Example B.1), and a demonstrated sharpness argument; the supporting Gaussian-envelope machinery (Proposition B.2, Lemma B.3) is standard but correctly deployed.

ACE is a principled generalization of Feynman–Kac correctors: Theorem 2.3 / A.1 derives the correct weighted SDE/ODE with auxiliary density-tracking dynamics for time-varying exponents, and FKC is recovered as a special case (γ̇=0), with clear algorithmic comparison (Algorithms 1 vs. 2).

Theorem B.2 gives a constructive proof that exponent schedules satisfying the criterion always exist (bump functions), and Corollary B.1 extends this to partial-support/heterogeneous-dimensional experts, which is the practically relevant case.

Empirical validation spans a controlled synthetic benchmark (5 seeds, W1/W2/MMD), a realistic drug-design task (flexible-pose scaffold decoration on CrossDocked2020 with DN/CONF/SBDD experts, beating both steering baselines and specialized monolithic models like AutoFragDiff/Delete), fragment linking, and a homogeneous image-composition setting (COCO-MIG), showing gains beyond collapse repair.

The prevalence study (125 schedule compositions, Table E.10; collapse rates 41%–80% as guidance increases) and the schedule survey (Tables E.7–E.9) convincingly establish that heterogeneity and collapse are the norm, not an edge case; ablations (time-varying schedules from prior work, schedule alignment via time reparameterization, bump-parameter sensitivity) credibly disentangle the contributions.

Limitations are discussed honestly and specifically (compact-support/Gaussian-interpolant scope, linear scaling in expert count, steering-not-repairing misaligned experts), and a reproducibility statement, compute details, hyperparameter tables, and code are provided.
weaknesses: The main theory is confined to Gaussian-prior-to-compactly-supported targets under Gaussian interpolation; the criterion's necessity direction does not transfer to general (e.g., heavy-tailed or non-Gaussian) priors, and the extension to mixed continuous–categorical molecular domains—which the drug-design experts arguably involve—is explicitly deferred to future work, weakening how directly the theory covers the flagship experiment.

The concentration result is stated informally in the main text (Proposition 2.1, 'Rt(ε) ≈ O(1/√C(t))') and the formal version (Proposition E.1) requires an a priori quadratic envelope and a uniform lower bound on Zt that are verified only in restricted settings; the bridge between 'sharper concentration' and observed sample quality is partly heuristic.

Theoretical path validity is only guaranteed up to a truncated t_end < 1, with the final segment handled by a single uncorrected Euler step; the O((1−t_end)²) error argument is plausible but informal, and the practical failure modes of collapsed paths (weight destabilization) are characterized empirically rather than quantitatively.

The empirical results exhibit notable sensitivity to the correction magnitude: in Tables 2/C.2–C.5 performance peaks at specific bump parameters and degrades substantially at larger B1 (e.g., B1=100 worse than no correction), showing that the guarantee of path existence does not translate into a guarantee of sample quality; the B2 values in the molecular experiments are chosen post hoc to satisfy the criterion.

The molecular evaluation is comparatively small-scale (76 pocket–scaffold pairs, five sampled molecules per pair, batch size 5; fragment linking with a single seed), and ACE-lite reintroduces bias, so the strongest headline results rest on a limited evaluation sample and some ablations use fewer seeds.

The methodological delta over Feynman–Kac correctors (Skreta et al., 2025a) is a natural extension—time-varying exponents plus a criterion-derived bump schedule—so the novelty rests chiefly on the collapse diagnosis and the criterion rather than on a new sampling primitive; the connection to the related time-varying guidance literature is handled, but the bump-function construction itself is fairly ad hoc.

Presentation: the main text is dense and heavily reliant on forward references to appendices for key details (sharpness of the criterion, formal concentration result, criterion-based hyperparameter selection), and some claims (e.g., 'reduces error by 4×') depend on the particular schedule configuration chosen for the synthetic benchmark.
